idiom_name: hand-written validate() gate called by the operation (return code plus caller-owned error struct)
implementation_notes: C has no constructors to trust, no exceptions and no standard validation layer, so the pattern is a convention: the struct holds whatever the parser produced, and a function such as int order_validate_for_publish(const struct order *o, struct err *e) is called by the operation about to use the object (write a file, enqueue a message, hand it to another subsystem). Failures travel back as return codes with a caller-owned detail struct, because errno - the libc convention in which a call reports failure immediately and the caller must inspect errno before any other library call - is usable only at the point of use and is easily clobbered. One use-named function per action, delegating to static helpers, is the honest replacement for a validator object; rebuild the object structure only when the same large rule set is shared by several operations.
pitfalls: errno is meaningful only immediately after the failing call and is clobbered by any later library call, so a deferred check must return its own status or fill a caller-owned struct instead of reading a stale errno.
The struct must record which fields were actually parsed (a qty_seen flag) or a zero-initialised field is indistinguishable from a legitimately absent one at validation time.
Ownership of error detail is undefined by convention: if the gate allocates the message, every caller must free it, and leaked or double-freed details are the usual outcome.
